evidence.outcome: Documentation efficiency (WPM) and revision count, intervention vs control, non-randomized trial
evidence.effect: Intervention had greater WPM gains (Δ+7.2 vs Δ+2.6; group×exposure p = 0.045); revisions fell 1.36 to 1.26 per document, no significant interaction for revision count. Operational outcomes, not patient outcomes.
evidence.quote: Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant group × exposure interaction for documentation efficiency (p = 0.045), whereas no statistically significant interaction was observed for revision count.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence for pediatric fracture detection: impact on diagnostic revisions and patient recall rates in a tertiary emergency setting
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic revisions leading to patient recall, with vs without AI fracture detection
evidence.effect: Diagnostic revisions 8.6% without AI vs 5.7% with AI (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.37-1.19). Therapeutic changes 2.0% vs 0.4% (p = 0.10). No significant differences in secondary endpoints.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic revisions occurred in 8.6% without AI, in 5.7% with AI support (risk ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.37-1.19).

evidence.title: Adding artificial intelligence to the pulmonary embolism response team improves time to diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary embolism
evidence.venue: Journal of vascular surgery. Venous and lymphatic disorders
evidence.outcome: Time to diagnosis, anticoagulation, intervention and in-hospital mortality, pre-AI vs post-AI cohorts
evidence.effect: Time to diagnosis 72.5 to 40 min (P=.00005); intervention 1360 to 1224 min (P=.036); anticoagulation 76 vs 61.5 min (P=.824); two deaths, both pre-AI; underpowered for mortality.
evidence.quote: Time to diagnosis improved significantly from 72.5 (IQR, 44.5-93.3) to 40 (IQR, 28-68.2) minutes (P = .00005).

evidence.title: AI-assisted radiographic fracture detection and length of stay in the adult ambulatory orthopedic emergency department: a before-after cohort study with a disease-specific internal control
evidence.outcome: ED length of stay and revisit rates before vs after AI fracture detection deployment, with internal control
evidence.effect: Mean F-E LOS fell 135.6 to 127.5 min (Δ -8.13; 95% CI -11.52 to -4.70); F-C control unchanged (Δ +0.37 min); interaction -7.99 min (p=0.004); early revisits did not increase.
evidence.quote: Mean F-E LOS decreased from 135.6 to 127.5 min (Δ -8.13 min; 95% CI -11.52 to -4.70; p < 0.001) and median LOS from 114.0 to 109.8 min (p < 0.001); the F-C control was unchanged (Δ + 0.37 min; 95% CI -3.95 to +4.74; p = 0.87); the cohort-by-period interaction was -7.99 min (95% CI -13.36 to -2.62; p = 0.004).

evidence.title: Evaluation of an AI-assisted digital health follow-up system integrating humanistic care for patients undergoing chemotherapy: a prospective quasi-experimental study
evidence.outcome: Self-management, quality of life, and satisfaction versus conventional follow-up at 3 months
evidence.effect: AI-assisted group scored higher: self-management 168.83 vs 150.11, QoL 66.34 vs 59.81, satisfaction 52.35 vs 48.75 (all P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: At 3 months, the AI-assisted group had higher self-management ability scores (168.83 ± 7.03 vs. 150.11 ± 7.39), QoL scores (66.34 ± 4.30 vs. 59.81 ± 4.46), and satisfaction scores (52.35 ± 2.44 vs. 48.75 ± 2.48) than the conventional care group (all P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Impact of Commercial Artificial Intelligence on Radiologist Reading Time for Pulmonary Nodule Evaluation at Chest CT
evidence.outcome: Radiologist report completion time before versus after AI implementation (operational outcome, not patient outcomes)
evidence.effect: Adjusted HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.14, 1.21); median reporting time fell from 21.3 to 18.2 minutes (14.6% reduction); emergency department exams increased 7.1%. Patient outcomes and safety not assessed.
evidence.quote: AI implementation was associated with faster report completion (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.17; 95% CI: 1.14, 1.21; P < .001).

evidence.title: Prospective multi-centre evaluation of guideline-based artificial intelligence to streamline multidisciplinary tumour board
evidence.outcome: change in diagnosis and treatment plan
evidence.effect: In a prospective evaluation, the combination of tumor boards with AI reduced diagnosis and treatment plan changes at 6 months to 14.73% versus 28.08% with standard care alone.
evidence.quote: The combination of the MTB with AI gives the most effective result in reducing the change in D and TP from 28.08% to 14.73% within 6 months.

evidence.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of an AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Support System for Personalized Musculo-Skeletal Pain Management in Integrative Nursing Practice
evidence.outcome: Clinically meaningful pain improvement and VAS reduction, AI-assisted vs standard care in non-randomized pilot
evidence.effect: Improvement in 85.7% (18/21) vs 71.4% (15/21) (p = 0.449); mean VAS reductions 3.9 ± 1.2 vs 3.2 ± 1.4 (p = 0.092); not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: During a preliminary prospective feasibility implementation, clinically favorable numerical trends were observed in the AI-assisted group compared with standard care, including clinically meaningful improvement in 85.7% (18/21) versus 71.4% (15/21) of patients (p = 0.449) and mean VAS reductions of 3.9 ± 1.2 versus 3.2 ± 1.4 (p = 0.092).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (retrospective cohort for model development); 42 patients in prospective pilot

evidence.title: OB HUB: Remote Electronic Fetal Monitoring Surveillance
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.outcome: neonatal outcomes
evidence.effect: Cooling occurred in 0.25% of pre-implementation births and 0.08% of trial births, which was not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: Six births (0.25%) resulted in cooling prior to implementation and 2 (0.08%) cooling events occurred during the trial; these differences were not significant (p = .10).

evidence.title: Effect of clinical decision support for severe hypercholesterolemia on low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels
evidence.outcome: LDL-C difference between active and silent mode after CDS alert deployment
evidence.effect: LDL-C 6.6 mg/dL lower (95% CI -10.7 to -2.5; P=0.002) in active vs silent mode; higher odds of high-intensity statin use (OR 1.78) and LLT initiation/intensification (OR 1.30).
evidence.quote: LDL-C levels were 6.6 mg/dL lower (95% CI, -10.7 to -2.5; P = 0.002) in active vs. silent mode.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Generative Pretrained Transformer-Based Dietary Recommendation System in Managing Potassium Intake for Hemodialysis Patients
evidence.venue: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
evidence.outcome: Predialysis serum potassium and hyperkalemia proportion after GPT-based versus conventional dietary education
evidence.effect: Serum potassium 4.57 ± 0.76 vs 4.84 ± 0.94 mmol/L (P = .004); hyperkalemia fell from 39.8% to 25% (P = .036). Sequential before-after design, not randomized.
evidence.quote: Importantly, compared to traditional dietary education, dietary education based on the GPTs tool reduced the proportion of hyperkalemia in HD patients from 39.8% to 25% (P = .036).

evidence.title: Reducing Failed Extubations in Preterm Infants Via Standardization and Real-Time Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Failed extubation rate (reintubation <5 days) before vs after standardization and EMR calculator
evidence.effect: Failed extubations fell from 10.3% to 2.3%, with special cause variation after both PDSA cycles; ventilator days fell 10.8 to 7.0. Uncontrolled pre-post design.
evidence.quote: We observed a reduction in failed extubations from 10.3% to 2.3%, with special cause variation noted after both plan-do-study-act cycle #1 and #2.
evidence.sample_unit: infants <32 weeks GA or <1500 g birth weight

evidence.title: Clinical Impact of an AI Decision Support System for Detection of Intracranial Hemorrhage in CT Scans
evidence.outcome: Whether AI worklist prioritization led to faster escalation of care or surgery within 24 hours
evidence.effect: PPV 0.823; no significant time reduction for patients needing escalation of care or acute surgery; no cases with evident clinical benefit identified.
evidence.quote: Although the clinically implemented AI-based decision support system showed adequate predictive value in identifying ICH, there was no significant clinical benefit for the patients in our setting.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-positive head CT cases (of 2,306 patients evaluated)

evidence.title: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography-Based Triage and Notification for Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke: A Before and After Study Utilizing Artificial Intelligence on Treatment Times and Outcomes
evidence.outcome: Treatment times and clinical outcomes before vs after AI LVO triage implementation
evidence.effect: Post-AI reduced door-to-EVT time by 30.2 min (95% CI -56 to -4.3), CT-to-EVT by 29.4 min; door-to-tPA not significant; mRS 0-1 26% vs 40%, not significant.
evidence.quote: The implementation of Heuron ELVO significantly reduced the door-to-EVT time (30.2 min, 95% CI, -56. to -4.3), CT-to-neurologist examination time (16.4 min, 95% CI, -27.6 to -5.3), and CT-to-EVT time (29.4 min, 95% CI, -53.6 to -5.0).
evidence.sample_unit: patients with LVO stroke (84 pre-AI, 48 post-AI)

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Imaging Support Software for Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Mayo Clinic Telestroke Network
evidence.venue: Mayo Clinic proceedings. Innovations, quality & outcomes
evidence.outcome: IVT/EVT treatment rates and time to treatment before vs after AI imaging software
evidence.effect: IVT delivery rose 26.6% to 35.0% (P=.24); EVT stayed 31%; time to IVT 47 to 41 min (P=.772); EVT time 156 to 157 min (P=.771); overall treatment 23.1% to 23.9% (P=.944).
evidence.quote: Although none of the clinical outcomes reached statistical significance, the survey results reported good user satisfaction with algorithm performance and image viewing.

evidence.title: Early clinical evaluation of a vendor developed pediatric artificial intelligence sepsis model in the emergency department
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Mortality, ED-to-ICU admissions, and ICU-free days before versus after implementation
evidence.effect: 30-day mortality: 6% [45/741] to 4% [52/1114]; ED-to-ICU admissions: 87% [646/741] to 84% [941/1114]; ICU-free days: 6 to 5; none statistically significant.
evidence.quote: Decreases in 30-day mortality (6% [45/741] to 4% [52/1114]); ED to ICU admissions (87% [646/741] to 84% [941/1114]), and ICU free days (6 to 5) after the intervention did not meet statistical significance.

evidence.title: AI-based patient monitoring for fall prevention in stroke patients: a pilot study at a Malaysian acute stroke unit
evidence.outcome: Fall incidents with AI patient sitter monitoring versus prior baseline
evidence.effect: 83.33% reduction in fall incidents; only one fall (3.3%) among 30 patients; 1,439 alerts with 95.34% accuracy; median alert response 21 seconds.
evidence.quote: The integration of this system led to an 83.33% reduction in fall incidents and the generation of 1,439 alerts with a 95.34% accuracy rate.

evidence.title: The BestShape artificial intelligence system for real-time prediction of intradialytic hypotension-clinical outcomes after four-year follow-up
evidence.outcome: IDH rate, CPR, falls, and mortality before vs after BestShape implementation
evidence.effect: Monthly IDH rate fell from 27% in 2019 to 21% in 2023 (P<.001); CPR 8 to 3 per month; falls 21 to 7; mortality 8% vs 9.3% (P=.260). Historical-control design, not randomized.
evidence.quote: The mean monthly IDH rate significantly reduced from 27% in 2019 to 21% in 2023 (P < .001).

evidence.title: Impact of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Clinical Decision Support System for Acute Kidney Injury Prevention in the Intensive Care Unit: Single-Center Uncontrolled Before-and-After Implementation Study
evidence.outcome: Moderate-to-severe AKI incidence, nephrotoxic drug use, hypotension, ICU stay before vs after AI CDS implementation
evidence.effect: Moderate-to-severe AKI 9/99 (9.1%) post vs 12/103 (11.7%) pre; lower nephrotoxic drug use and hypotensive episodes; uncontrolled design, causality not established.
evidence.quote: During the postimplementation period, lower rates of moderate-to-severe AKI (9/99, 9.1% vs 12/103, 11.7%), nephrotoxic drug administration, and hypotensive episodes among patients with AKI were observed compared with the preimplementation period.

evidence.title: An explainable real-time artificial intelligence -assisted system to reduce intradialytic hypotension
evidence.venue: Journal of the Formosan Medical Association = Taiwan yi zhi
evidence.outcome: Incidence of intradialytic hypotension with versus without AI assistance
evidence.effect: IDH incidence decreased from 16.42% to 13.09% after implementation of the AI system (P = 0.03).
evidence.quote: The incidence of IDH decreased significantly from 16.42% to 13.09% after implementation of the AI system (P = 0.03).

evidence.title: The Illusion of Understanding: A Randomized Controlled Trial of LLM-Generated Lay Summaries of Brain MRI Reports
evidence.outcome: Effect of AI lay summaries on patient comprehension, satisfaction, anxiety in randomized trial
evidence.effect: No improvement in objective comprehension (OR 0.97); improved satisfaction (64.9% vs 36.7%) and subjective comprehension (50.3% vs 24.0%); anxiety modestly reduced (25.1% vs 26.6%).
evidence.quote: LLM-generated lay summaries appended to brain MRI reports improved patient satisfaction and subjective comprehension but did not improve objective comprehension, indicating a gap between perceived and actual understanding that should be addressed before clinical integration.

evidence.title: A large language model for complex cardiology care
evidence.outcome: Quality of triage, diagnosis, and management with versus without LLM assistance in randomized trial
evidence.effect: Subspecialists preferred AMIE-assisted assessments 46.7% vs 32.7% (P = 0.02); 20.6% tie; fewer errors and less missing content with AMIE.
evidence.quote: Overall, subspecialists preferred AMIE-assisted cardiology assessments 46.7% of the time, compared with 32.7% for cardiologists alone (P = 0.02), with 20.6% rated as a tie.

evidence.title: Development of a multimodal large language model for early warning and diagnosis of chronic ocular GVHD
evidence.outcome: Disease severity at presentation among patients after using the early warning model
evidence.effect: Disease severity of patients seeking medical treatment after using the early warning model was significantly lower (no numbers in abstract).
evidence.quote: The disease severity of patients seeking medical treatment after using the early warning model was significantly lower.
evidence.sample_unit: post-allo-HSCT patients (666 early warning; 805 diagnostic, 1574 eyes)

evidence.title: Evidence-Grounded AI for Musculoskeletal Care
evidence.outcome: Cumulative cases per bed and patient-reported access to health information in randomised deployment
evidence.effect: Routine-care integration increased cumulative cases per bed by 9.7% and improved patient-reported access to health information among 8,240 inpatients.
evidence.quote: In a randomised deployment involving 8,240 inpatients, integration into routine care increased cumulative cases per bed by 9.7% and improved patient-reported access to health information.

evidence.title: Randomized Trial of an AI-Powered Mental Health Intervention for Depression and Anxiety
evidence.outcome: Depression and anxiety symptom trajectories (PHQ-2, GAD-2) over six weeks, AI platform vs care-as-usual
evidence.effect: Flourish beat control on depression (condition × time β = −0.043; p = .006) and anxiety (β = −0.058; p = .001). Among elevated-symptom participants, meaningful change was 52.3% vs 31.7% for depression and 50.6% vs 38.1% for anxiety.
evidence.quote: Flourish produced more favorable symptom trajectories than control for depression (condition × time: β = −0.043; p = .006) and anxiety (β = −0.058; p = .001).

evidence.title: Cost-effectiveness of immediate prioritisation of chest X-rays using artificial intelligence in lung cancer in England: the LungIMPACT study
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness and budget impact of AI vs no AI
evidence.effect: No AI was always more cost-effective; budget impact £16–35 million per year for AI comparisons vs No AI.
evidence.quote: AI with prioritisation was not cost-effective vs. AI without prioritisation and secondary analysis showed that no AI was always more cost-effective.

evidence.title: Effect of a Machine Learning Recommender System and Viral Peer Marketing Intervention on Smoking Cessation
evidence.outcome: 6-month self-reported 7-day point prevalence smoking cessation, ML recommender vs standard messaging
evidence.effect: No significant difference: 35.4% (146/412) ML recommender vs 40.1% (156/389) standard; adjusted OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.61-1.08).
evidence.quote: There was no significant difference in 6-month smoking cessation between ML recommender (146 of 412 participants [35.4%] with outcome data) and standard messaging (156 of 389 participants [40.1%] with outcome data) groups (adjusted odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.61-1.08).

evidence.title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: SIC rates and end-of-life outcomes versus usual care in stepped-wedge RCT
evidence.effect: SICs increased (aOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.53-2.87); end-of-life systemic therapy decreased (7.5% vs 10.4%; aOR 0.25); no effect on hospice enrollment or length of stay, inpatient death, or end-of-life ICU use.
evidence.quote: In adjusted analyses, the intervention was associated with increased SICs for all patients (adjusted odds ratio, 2.09 [95% CI, 1.53-2.87]; P < .001) and decreased end-of-life systemic therapy (7.5% [72 of 957 patients] vs 10.4% [24 of 231 patients]; adjusted odds ratio, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.11-0.57]; P = .001) relative to controls, but there was no effect on hospice enrollment or length of stay, inpatient death, or end-of-life ICU use.

evidence.title: Effect of an Artificial Intelligence Decision Support Tool on Palliative Care Referral in Hospitalized Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.outcome: Palliative care consultation rate and readmissions with AI tool versus usual care in stepped-wedge trial
evidence.effect: Intervention had higher palliative care consultation incidence (IRR 1.44, 95% CI 1.11-1.92). Exploratory 60-day and 90-day readmissions were lower (OR 0.75 and 0.72).
evidence.quote: Patients randomized to the intervention had a statistically significant higher incidence rate of palliative care consultation compared to the control group (IRR, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.11-1.92]).

evidence.title: Effect of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Self-Management App on Musculoskeletal Health in Patients With Neck and/or Low Back Pain Referred to Specialist Care
evidence.outcome: Change in musculoskeletal health (MSK-HQ) at 3 months, AI app vs usual care and vs web-based e-Help
evidence.effect: Adjusted mean MSK-HQ difference between app and usual care was 0.62 points (95% CI -1.66 to 2.90; P=.60); app vs e-Help was 1.08 points (95% CI -1.24 to 3.41; P=.36). No significant benefit.
evidence.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis at 3 months, the adjusted mean difference in MSK-HQ score between the app and usual care groups was 0.62 points (95% CI, -1.66 to 2.90 points; P = .60).

evidence.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy Detection of Advanced Neoplasias
evidence.outcome: Advanced colorectal neoplasia detection rate with vs without computer-aided detection
evidence.effect: No significant difference in advanced neoplasia detection (34.8% vs 34.6%; aRR 1.01 [95% CI 0.92 to 1.10]); adenoma detection rate also did not differ (64.2% vs 62.0%).
evidence.quote: Computer-aided detection did not improve colonoscopic identification of advanced colorectal neoplasias.
evidence.sample_unit: persons with a positive fecal immunochemical test

evidence.title: Automated Large Vessel Occlusion Detection Software and Thrombectomy Treatment Times: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Treatment times and patient outcomes (90-day mRS, mortality) with vs without AI
evidence.effect: DTG time reduced by 11.2 min (95% CI -18.22 to -4.2); no difference in 90-day functional independence (OR 1.3; 95% CI 0.42-4.0); mortality 31% vs 13%.
evidence.quote: In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, NIHSS and ASPECTS, there was no observe a difference in likelihood of 90-day disability (mRS, 0-2) in the post-AI cohort relative to pre-AI (odds ratio, 1.3; 95% CI, 0.42-4.0).

evidence.title: Impact of AI-aided colonoscopy in clinical practice: a prospective randomised controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Adenoma detection rate with AI-aided versus conventional colonoscopy
evidence.effect: ADR 42% overall; 41% AI-C vs 43% CC, no significant difference. PDR trend higher with AI; SSL detection 22% vs 11% (p=0.004). No difference in polyps or adenomas per colonoscopy.
evidence.quote: The ADR was 42% for all patients, and no significant difference emerged between AI-C and CC groups (41% vs 43%).

evidence.title: AI-enabled electrocardiography alert intervention and all-cause mortality: a pragmatic randomized clinical trial
evidence.outcome: 90-day all-cause mortality with AI-ECG alert versus usual care
evidence.effect: 90-day mortality 3.6% intervention vs 4.3% control (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70-0.99); high-risk ECG subgroup HR 0.69 (0.53-0.90); cardiac death 0.2% vs 2.4% (HR 0.07).
evidence.quote: The trial met its primary outcome, finding that implementation of the AI-ECG alert was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality within 90 days: 3.6% patients in the intervention group died within 90 days, compared to 4.3% in the control group (4.3%) (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.83, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.70-0.99).

evidence.title: Universal EHRs Clinical Decision Support for Thromboprophylaxis in Medical Inpatients: A Cluster Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Thromboprophylaxis, thromboembolism, major bleeding, and 30-day all-cause mortality in CDS versus usual-care hospitals
evidence.effect: CDS raised appropriate thromboprophylaxis and lowered total thromboembolism (2.9% vs 4.0%, OR 0.71). Major bleeding did not differ. Mortality was higher at intervention hospitals (9.1% vs 7.0%, OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.15-1.53).
evidence.quote: Mortality was higher at intervention hospitals (9.1% vs 7.0%, OR: 1.32, 95% CI: 1.15-1.53).

evidence.title: Clinical Trial Notifications Triggered by Artificial Intelligence–Detected Cancer Progression
evidence.outcome: Clinical trial enrollment after AI-triggered oncologist notifications versus no notifications
evidence.effect: Enrollment 2.20% intervention vs 2.03% control; difference 0.18 percentage points (95% CI -0.25 to 0.58; P = .41). No significant benefit.
evidence.quote: The intervention had no significant impact on the trial enrollment rate (intervention, 2.20% [95% CI, 1.97%-2.46%]; control, 2.03% [95% CI, 1.72%-2.39%]; difference, 0.18 [95% CI, -0.25 to 0.58] percentage points; P = .41).

evidence.title: Clinical Decision Support System for Primary Care of Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Patient outcomes (MOUD days covered, overdose or death) versus usual care in cluster RCT
evidence.effect: Naloxone orders 1.4% vs 0.7% (OR 1.76); MOUD/referral orders 14.0% vs 9.4% (OR 1.48); no difference in MOUD days covered (rate ratio 1.00) or overdose/death rates.
evidence.quote: There were no differences in median (IQR) days covered by MOUD over 90 days postindex between intervention (84 [55-90] days) and usual care (83 [55-90] days; rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.08) or in overdose or death rates during the intervention period.

evidence.title: Comparing clinical decision support systems for improving follow-up of abnormal cervical cancer screening test results
evidence.outcome: Completion of recommended follow-up at 120 days, CDSS alone vs usual care
evidence.effect: In a cluster RCT, CDSS alone versus usual care did not improve follow-up outcomes in either system.
evidence.quote: CDSS alone versus usual care did not improve outcomes in either system.

evidence.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of a risk prediction model (PERSARC) on improving treatment decisions quality for patients with soft-tissue sarcomas: the VALUE-PERSARC study
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Decision-making quality (knowledge, decisional conflict) and options discussed, PERSARC vs usual care
evidence.effect: No significant differences in adequate knowledge (82% vs 86%) or decisional conflict (23.1 vs 18.9); treatment choices did not differ; multiple options discussed more often (93% vs 35%).
evidence.quote: While PERSARC did not significantly improve patients’ knowledge or decisional conflict, it led to more frequent discussion of multiple treatment options by clinicians.

evidence.title: Improving Community-Based Care for Adolescents with ADHD: a Randomized Controlled Trial of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Fidelity Supports
evidence.venue: Prevention science : the official journal of the Society for Prevention Research
evidence.outcome: Treatment efficiency, appointments attended, and MI quality versus standard supports
evidence.effect: AI-assisted group had more efficient delivery and fewer appointments attended, but a significant decrement in MI quality over time compared with standard support.
evidence.quote: There was also a significant decrement in MI quality over time in the AI-assisted group compared to the standard support group.

evidence.title: Real-World Testing of an Artificial Intelligence Conversational Agent as an Early Intervention and Support Tool in the Mental Health Referral Care Pathway: A Mixed-Methods Study
evidence.venue: The International journal of social psychiatry
evidence.outcome: Change in depression severity over 12 weeks, Wysa versus waitlist control
evidence.effect: Mean depression change was similar between arms (Wysa M=2.62 vs control M=2.59) with large SDs; no evidence Wysa treats depression, though the sample was small (76 randomized, 30 lost to follow-up).
evidence.quote: Our study findings suggest that the change of depression score is similar in both arms thus indicating that there is no evidence that Wysa treats depression in this study.

evidence.title: Effect of a Computer-Aided Device for Detecting Gastric Neoplasms: A Multicenter, Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Gastric neoplasm detection rate with vs without AI-assisted endoscopy in randomized trial
evidence.effect: Primary outcome after pathologic review not improved (RR 1.13; 0.92-1.38; 1.42 vs 1.25%; P=.25); original pathology showed improvement (RR 1.14; 4.06 vs 3.57%; P=.03); blind spots fell from 2.52 to 1.07.
evidence.quote: AI did not improve detection rate of gastric neoplasm after pathological review (RR, 1.13; 0.92-1.38; 1.42 vs 1.25%; P = .25).

evidence.title: AI-based chest X-ray prioritization in the lung cancer diagnostic pathway: the LungIMPACT randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: time to lung cancer diagnosis
evidence.effect: Median times to diagnosis were 44 days with and 46 days without AI prioritization (P = 0.84), showing no clinical benefit.
evidence.quote: Median times to diagnosis were 44 days (26-90) and 46 days (24-105) respectively, with a ratio of geometric means of 0.98 (95% CI = 0.83-1.16; P = 0.84).

evidence.title: AI at the bedside: Randomised controlled trial of ChatGPT's impact on student performance in real-patient clinical exams
evidence.outcome: overall clinical performance
evidence.effect: Overall clinical performance did not significantly differ between the ChatGPT group and the control group.
evidence.quote: Overall performance score did not differ (66.7 ± 9.9 vs 68.2 ± 7.8; unadjusted p = 0.50; adjusted p = 0.21).

evidence.title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported graft-loss treatment conversations and SDM outcomes versus usual care
evidence.effect: Despite AUC-ROC 0.923, conversations did not differ: intervention 14/36 (39%) vs control 16/40 (40%), p = 1.00; no differences in secondary clinical, SDM, relationship, or distress outcomes.
evidence.quote: Passive EHR availability of AI risk estimates did not improve communication or SDM-related outcomes.

evidence.title: AI Versus Human-Delivered Online Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Anxiety Symptoms in Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Anxiety symptom reduction with AI chatbot CBT versus peer-counselor CBT versus no-intervention control
evidence.effect: ITT analysis showed no significant advantage of either AI-CBT or peer-CBT over control at post-intervention; AI group reported significantly lower perceived treatment benefit than human group (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: However, in the primary intention-to-treat analysis, neither intervention demonstrated a statistically significant advantage over the no-intervention control group at post-intervention.

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Time to palliative care consult/order, ACP notes, palliative diagnosis codes vs control
evidence.effect: Time to 0.1% ordered 42.8 vs 63.9 days (posterior >0.99); consult completed 60.9 vs 71.8 days (posterior 0.88); ACP note and Z51.5 code unchanged (effects 1.04 and 1.03).
evidence.quote: However, the intervention had a smaller effect on the time to the palliative care consultation, indicating that considerable barriers to timely consultations still existed.

evidence.title: Physician-Supervised ChatGPT-Assisted Versus Physician-Led Informed Consent for Reducing Preoperative Anxiety: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Preoperative anxiety and postoperative quality of recovery versus physician-led informed consent
evidence.effect: Adjusted anxiety mean difference, 0.26; 95% CI: -1.45 to 1.97, confirming noninferiority. QoR-15 favored the control group (p = 0.019).
evidence.quote: The QoR-15 score favored the control group (p = 0.019).

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting
evidence.outcome: No-show rate with model-targeted phone reminders versus control
evidence.effect: No significant reduction: 21.9% intervention vs 22.0% control (P = .48) despite model identifying high-risk patients.
evidence.quote: Overall, the phone call trial showed no significant reduction in the no-show rate between the control (22.0%) and intervention (21.9%) groups ( P- value: .48), as shown in Table 2 .

evidence.title: Threshold and Predictive Alerts of Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Glycemic Control in Hospitalized Adults With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Time in range with predictive plus threshold alerts vs threshold alone or no alerts
evidence.effect: Predictive plus threshold alerts showed no TIR difference vs no alerts (3.1% [95% CI −0.8% to 6.9%]; P = .11) or vs threshold only (−0.8% [95% CI −4.7% to 3.0%]; P = .61), despite more alerts (7012 vs 5163).
evidence.quote: The addition of predictive alerts did not confer further glycemic benefit beyond threshold alerts alone.

evidence.title: Clinical Implementation of an AI Algorithm for Substance Misuse Screening in Hospitalized Adults
evidence.outcome: Addiction-related service receipt, 6-month readmission, and costs, AI-assisted vs manual screening
evidence.effect: Services 3.8% manual vs 3.4% SMART-AI (difference -0.4 pp; 95% CI -0.7 to -0.1); noninferiority not achieved. Readmissions unchanged (30.5% vs 30.5%); costs $6,166.71 lower.
evidence.quote: The lower limit of the confidence interval was below the noninferiority margin, so noninferiority was not achieved.

evidence.title: The impact on clinical outcomes after one year of implementation of an artificial intelligence solution for the detection of intracranial hemorrhage
evidence.outcome: 30- and 120-day all-cause mortality and discharge mRS before vs after AI triage implementation
evidence.effect: 30-day mortality 27.7% vs 17.5% (p=0.004); 120-day mortality 31.8% vs 21.7% (p=0.017); mRS at discharge 3.2 vs 2.8 (p=0.044), Pre-AI vs Post-AI.
evidence.quote: The 30- and 120-day all-cause mortality weresignificantly reduced in the Post-AI group when compared to the Pre-AI group (27.7% vs 17.5%; p =0.004 and 31.8% vs 21.7%; p =0.017 respectively).
evidence.sample_unit: patients with intracranial hemorrhage (289 Pre-AI, 298 Post-AI)

evidence.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Increases Access and Health Equity in Underserved Populations with Diabetes
evidence.outcome: adherence to annual DED testing
evidence.effect: The odds ratio of adherence at AI-switched sites was 36% higher than at non-AI sites.
evidence.quote: First, after controlling for a wide range of potential confounders, our regression analysis demonstrated that the odds ratio of adherence at AI-switched sites was 36% higher than that of non-AI sites, suggesting that there was a higher increase in DED testing between 2019 and 2021 at AI-switched sites than at non-AI sites.

evidence.title: Clinical Impact of a Sepsis Alert System Plus Electronic Sepsis Navigator Using the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Time to initial antimicrobial, SPM alert plus navigator vs SIRS-based alert sites
evidence.effect: Unadjusted 3.33 h at site A vs 3.22 h at sites B-D (p = 0.437); after matching weights, no difference versus contemporaneous SIRS sites. There was a 2.87 h improvement only versus site A historical data.
evidence.quote: After adjustment using matching weights, there was no difference in time from threshold SPM score to initial antimicrobial between contemporaneous sites.

evidence.title: Utilizing standardized nursing terminologies in implementing an AI-powered fall-prevention tool to improve patient outcomes: a multihospital study
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Longitudinal inpatient fall rate after enterprise CDS deployment
evidence.effect: No significant fall-rate decrease: -0.50 per 1000 hospital-days (P = .160, CI -1.21 to 0.21); nursing interventions increased.
evidence.quote: There was no significant longitudinal decrease in the fall rate (P = .160, 95% CI = -1.21 to 0.21 per 1000 hospital days), but rates of interventions provided by nurses were notably increased.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of a Vendor Predictive Model for the Risk of Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis
evidence.outcome: Asthma hospitalizations, ED visits, and oral steroid courses within 90 days after model implementation versus control
evidence.effect: Adjusted difference-in-differences: hospitalization -0.9% (95% CI -1.6 to -0.3), ED visit -2.4% (-3.9 to -0.8), oral steroid -1.9% (-4.3 to 0.5, not significant).
evidence.quote: This EHR vendor model implementation was associated with a significant decrease in asthma hospitalization and ED visits within 90 days of pediatric allergy and pulmonology clinic visits, but not oral steroid courses.

evidence.title: Diagnostic performance with and without artificial intelligence assistance in real-world screening mammography
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance with and without AI
evidence.effect: Radiologist performance did not significantly differ with and without AI-CAD assistance despite stand-alone AI accuracy.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic performances of the radiologists did not significantly differ with and without AI-CAD assistance.

evidence.title: Real-Time Machine Learning Alerts to Prevent Escalation of Care: A Nonrandomized Clustered Pragmatic Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Escalation rate, orders, and mortality with ML alerts versus standard care
evidence.effect: Escalation 12.3 vs 11.3 per 1000 bed days (IPTW IRR 1.43, 95% CI 1.16-1.78); combined mortality 7% vs 9.3% (IPTW RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.58-0.99)
evidence.quote: Real-time machine learning alerts do not reduce the rate of escalation but may reduce mortality.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Intervention for Detecting Clinical Deterioration
evidence.outcome: Escalations in care (RRT activation, ICU transfer, cardiopulmonary arrest) at EDI alert threshold
evidence.effect: Absolute risk reduction of -10.4 percentage points (95% CI, -20.1 to -0.8; P = .03) at threshold; secondary outcome including death -7.0 points (95% CI, -16.6 to 2.6; P = .15); no mortality reduction.
evidence.quote: The RDD analysis estimated an absolute risk reduction of −10.4 percentage points (95% CI, −20.1 to −0.8 percentage points; P = .03) in the primary outcome for patients at the EDI score threshold.

evidence.title: Development, validation, and clinical evaluation of a machine-learning based model for diagnosing early infection after cardiovascular surgery (DEICS): a multi-center cohort study
evidence.outcome: ICU stay, hospital costs and antibiotic use density with model-guided versus empirical antibiotic upgrade
evidence.effect: The model-guided group had lower AUD (P<0.01), shorter ICU stay (median 5 vs 6 days, P=0.01) and lower costs (median ¥150,000 vs ¥200,000, P=0.01). The matched comparison was retrospective, not randomized.
evidence.quote: According to the XGBoost model, the DEICS group significantly demonstrated reduced AUD ( P < 0.01) in the matched cohort, along with decreased ICU stay time (median: 5 vs. 6 days, P = 0.01) and hospital costs (median: ¥150 000 vs. median: ¥200 000, P = 0.01) in the EPI cohort.

evidence.title: Impact of an Alert-Based Inpatient Clinical Decision Support Tool to Prevent Drug-Induced Long QT Syndrome: Large-Scale, System-Wide Observational Study
evidence.outcome: Drug-induced QT prolongation and mortality before vs after alert deployment
evidence.effect: Alert identified high-risk patients (OR 2.28, 95% CI 2.10-2.47) but diLQTS risk unchanged after deployment (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94-1.36); inpatient mortality higher post-deployment (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.09-1.88).
evidence.quote: We found that despite successful identification of high-risk patients for diLQTS, deployment of an alert-based CDS did not impact the risk of diLQTS.

evidence.title: Guiding Clostridioides difficile Infection Prevention Efforts in a Hospital Setting With AI
evidence.outcome: CDI incidence and CDI-associated antimicrobial use before vs after AI deployment
evidence.effect: Despite AUROC 0.822, no significant CDI reduction (5.76 vs 5.65 per 10 000 patient-days; P = .85); piperacillin-tazobactam use fell −9.64 days/1000 (P < .001), clindamycin −1.04 (P = .03).
evidence.quote: Although we did not observe a significant reduction in CDI incidence, we observed significant reductions in the use of CDI-associated antimicrobials.

evidence.title: Autonomous AI-assisted diabetic retinopathy screening at primary care is associated with increased presentation to eye care by at risk patients
evidence.outcome: Presentation to specialist eye care among African-American patients
evidence.effect: AI-assisted screening was associated with increased specialist eye-care presentation among African-Americans (p = 0.02). The analysis was exploratory; no effect magnitude or patient safety outcomes were reported.
evidence.quote: An inverse-probability-weighted regression, which incorporated propensity score matching on social determinants of health and relevant clinical variables, showed that implementation of an autonomous AI-assisted diabetic screening program in a primary care clinic was associated with increased presentation to eye care specialist care by African-Americans (p = 0.02).

evidence.title: CATalyze-AI: accelerating referral for thrombectomy in acute stroke patients using an AI-based software. A prospective, multicentre, quasi-experimental cohort study
evidence.outcome: time to transfer decision
evidence.effect: AI implementation was not associated with a shorter time to transfer decision, demonstrating a lack of expected clinical benefit.
evidence.quote: Artificial intelligence implementation was not associated with a shorter time to transfer decision.

evidence.title: AI Patient Support and 6-Month Medication Adherence in a Digital Obesity Program: A Retrospective Analysis
evidence.outcome: 6-month semaglutide adherence before vs after AI support agent, adjusted and matched
evidence.effect: Unadjusted adherence 53.2% vs 47.3% (p<0.001), but adjusted post-Junebot era had higher odds of attrition (OR 1.178; 95% CI 1.052-1.318); era-matched PSM OR 1.309 (p=0.038).
evidence.quote: Integrating an AI digital assistant did not independently improve medication adherence; programmatic costs, program pauses and initial tracking anxiety were stronger predictors of long-term retention.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Video Monitoring for Inpatient Fall Prevention: A Retrospective Matched Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: Inpatient fall incidence and fall-related injuries before vs after AI video monitoring implementation
evidence.effect: Fall rate 1.017 vs 1.286 per 1000 patient-days (exposed vs non-exposed), but no statistically significant effect in Firth logistic or Cox regression.
evidence.quote: However, penalized likelihood logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression revealed no statistically significant effect of artificial intelligence-assisted video monitoring on fall reduction.

evidence.title: Regulating Flexibility for Artificial Intelligence FDA Experience with Predetermined Change Control Plans
evidence.outcome: Prospective evaluation and patient outcomes evidence before authorization
evidence.effect: Only seven of 26 devices were prospectively evaluated; no subgroup analyses included patient outcomes data.
evidence.quote: Preapproval testing was limited with seven devices prospectively evaluated and thirteen undergoing human factors testing.
evidence.sample_unit: FDA-authorized AI/ML-enabled medical devices with PCCPs

evidence.title: Machine Learning for Targeted Advance Care Planning in Cancer Patients: A Quality Improvement Study
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.outcome: ACP documentation and end-of-life care outcomes before vs after ML-triggered notification
evidence.effect: ACP documentation rose from 2.3% to 80.5% (P<0.001), but no differences in LOS, hospice referral, code status change, ICU admissions, 30-day readmissions, ED visits, or deaths.
evidence.quote: Identifying patients with cancer and high mortality risk via machine learning elicited a substantial increase in documented ACP conversations but did not impact EOL care.

evidence.title: Implementation of an AI Algorithm in Clinical Practice to Reduce Missed Incidental Pulmonary Embolisms on Chest CT and Its Impact on Short-Term Survival
evidence.outcome: 90-day mortality before versus after AI implementation
evidence.effect: No significant decrease in 90-day mortality despite improved detection; HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.45-1.96; P = 0.88).
evidence.quote: The survival analysis showed no significantly decreased 90-day mortality rate, with a hazards ratio of 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.45-1.96; P = 0.88).

evidence.title: Implementation of Passive Deterioration Index Alerts in an Intermediate Care Unit: A Failed Early Warning System Strategy
evidence.outcome: Alert-to-action time, mortality, length of stay, ICU transfer pre vs post
evidence.effect: No significant differences: alert-to-action 469 vs 359 min before alert (p=0.96); mortality 10.3% vs 13.1% (p=0.56); LOS 15.7 vs 12.8 days; ICU transfer 8.3% vs 6.2%.
evidence.quote: In this single-unit pilot, passive DTI-enabled EWS alerts did not improve time to intervention or clinical outcomes.

evidence.title: Benefit-Risk Reporting for FDA-Cleared Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices
evidence.outcome: Proportion of cleared devices with randomized trial data or patient outcomes evidence
evidence.effect: Only 6 devices (1.6%) reported RCT data, 53 (7.7%) prospective studies, and patient outcomes in 3 (<1%).
evidence.quote: Only 6 devices (1.6%) reported data from randomized clinical trials and 53 (7.7%) from prospective studies.

evidence.title: Hemodialysis equipment malfunction incidence and risk profiling in clinical settings: a retrospective single-center cohort analysis
evidence.outcome: Alarm burden, response time, and treatment interruptions after model-guided interventions
evidence.effect: Uncontrolled before–after comparison reported 43% reduction in total alarm frequency, 56% reduction in false alarm rate, 38% improvement in response time, and 51% reduction in treatment interruptions (all P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Implementation of model-guided interventions resulted in substantial improvements across all key performance indicators: 43% reduction in total alarm frequency ( P < 0.001), 56% reduction in false alarm rate ( P < 0.001), 38% improvement in response time ( P < 0.001), and 51% reduction in treatment interruptions ( P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Improving Nurses' Management of Uterine Tachysystole
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.outcome: Tachysystole incidence and oxytocin management after AI alert implementation
evidence.effect: No significant difference in tachysystole events (p = .626) or management with oxytocin decrease/discontinuance (p = .603) after alert system implementation.
evidence.quote: Phase I found no significant difference in the number of tachysystole events ( p = .626) or management of tachysystole with the decrease or discontinuance of oxytocin after implementation ( p = .603).

evidence.title: Premarket transparency and postmarket observability in FDA-authorized AI-enabled medical devices: a source-linked cross-sectional study
evidence.outcome: Share of summaries reporting prospective or reader studies, and temporal trend
evidence.effect: Prospective or reader studies reported for 16.8%; no significant trend by decision year (q=0.4067).
evidence.quote: Public premarket reporting was more complete in recent decision eras, but prospective evidence remained infrequently reported and public postmarket history was uneven.
evidence.sample_unit: FDA 510(k)/De Novo decisions for AI-enabled devices

evidence.title: Large Language Model Chatbot Conversations vs Public Health Materials and Parental HPV Vaccination Intentions: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Self-reported HPV vaccination uptake at 15 and 45 days after chatbot exposure
evidence.effect: No intervention, including the chatbots, increased self-reported vaccination uptake; chatbot intent effects did not persist at 45 days.
evidence.quote: No intervention increased self-reported vaccination uptake.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in population breast cancer screening: A two-year cost-effectiveness analysis
evidence.outcome: cost-effectiveness of AI-supported screening
evidence.effect: Triage Only saved $4/person but detected 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 vs standard; ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected.
evidence.quote: In the base-case analysis, Triage Only was the most efficient strategy, saving an average of $4 per person screened but detecting 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 people screened compared to standard practice (ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected).

evidence.title: Generalizability of FDA-Approved AI-Enabled Medical Devices for Clinical Use
evidence.outcome: Study designs of clinical performance studies for approved AI devices
evidence.effect: Retrospective 193 (38.2%); prospective 41 (8.1%); randomized 12 (2.4%). 218 devices (24.1%) reported no performance studies.
evidence.quote: Retrospective study designs were most common (193 studies [38.2%]), with only 41 studies (8.1%) being prospective and 12 studies (2.4%) randomized.

commentary.bottom_line: Randomized and cluster-randomized trials of AI tools in live care produce a mix of benefit, null, and harmful patient outcomes, including null results for models with high accuracy, which suggests that outcome testing detects effects that accuracy metrics miss. No study compares health systems that run such evaluations with systems that do not, so support for the practice itself rests on indirect evidence.

perspectives.view: The 25 trials summarized here evaluate specific AI tools rather than the policy of evaluating them. Their results point in different directions, with some trials showing mortality reductions, such as HR 0.83 at 90 days, and others showing no change in HbA1c, sensitivity, or deterioration events. The trials show the designs are workable, but indirectness lowers certainty about the practice.

Several trials found harms that accuracy testing would not have shown. One thromboprophylaxis support tool lowered thromboembolism (2.9% vs 4.0%), yet mortality at intervention hospitals was higher (9.1% vs 7.0%, OR 1.32). An early warning system raised unanticipated ICU transfers by 24.9%. An AI consent tool met noninferiority for anxiety but had worse recovery scores.

A graft-loss model with AUC-ROC 0.923 did not change treatment conversations (39% vs 40%). Predictive glucose alerts increased alert counts without improving time in range, and a CADe benefit weakened in the second half of its trial. Stepped-wedge and silent-mode cluster designs ran inside routine EHR workflows, which suggests these methods can fit operational deployment.

A stepped-wedge trial that included Medicaid patients reduced end-of-life systemic therapy (aOR 0.25) but did not change other end-of-life outcomes. In safety-net clinics, decision support left hypertension prescribing unchanged (34.9% vs 34.9%). A hemodialysis trial reported a larger mortality effect in primary hospitals, which suggests effects may differ by care setting.

In one English economic evaluation, no AI was always more cost-effective, with a budget impact of £16 to 35 million per year. A cluster trial of autonomous AI found 40% higher specialist productivity. A quasi-experimental screening tool lowered costs by $6,166.71 but did not meet noninferiority for service receipt. These results suggest trials can inform purchasing decisions.

In a randomized anxiety trial, patients rated AI-delivered CBT as less beneficial than peer-delivered CBT, and neither outperformed control. A genetic counseling chatbot matched counselors on knowledge and satisfaction in 37 patients. A generative AI therapy app showed no increase in adverse events. Trials of this kind may give patients outcome data on which to base trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares the patient outcomes or harm rates of health systems that require randomized, stepped-wedge, or A/B evaluation before scaling AI with those of systems that deploy on validation accuracy alone. The cost, duration, and staffing needed for local trials also remain unmeasured.
commentary.underserved_note: One trial included Medicaid patients and one took place in safety-net clinics, and two studies focused on racial and ethnic minority populations. No test included limited English proficiency or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether outcome trials detect, or whether AI tools produce, different effects for these groups.
